title: Grace That Teaches Us to Live
summary: Paul tells Titus to teach what fits sound doctrine, giving instructions for older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself, and slaves, each shaped so that the gospel will not be discredited but made attractive. He grounds all of it in the grace of God that has appeared, bringing salvation, which trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live upright lives while they wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. Christ gave himself to redeem a people eager to do good.
story: Chapter 1 dealt with leaders and with false teachers who professed God but denied him by their deeds. Chapter 2 turns to the whole congregation and shows what sound teaching looks like in ordinary lives. Paul moves through the household group by group, and at the end he explains why: because the grace of God has appeared in Christ and is shaping a people for his own possession. The chapter answers the false teachers not only with correct words but with transformed households. What the opponents deny by their actions, the church is to display by its good works.
historical:
The churches on Crete, like early churches everywhere, met in households, and their members lived within the ordinary structures of Greco-Roman society: families headed by husbands and fathers, and households that often included slaves. Christianity was new and suspected. Outsiders watched Christian households closely, and critics of the movement accused it of disrupting families and encouraging slaves and women to defy the social order. Paul's repeated purpose clauses show his concern with that scrutiny: so that the word of God will not be discredited (verse 5), so that opponents will have nothing bad to say (verse 8), so that slaves will adorn the teaching (verse 10).

Slavery was common across the Roman world, including on Crete. Slaves could be household servants, managers, or laborers, and pilfering from a master was a common complaint in ancient literature. For the background of slavery and how the New Testament addresses it, see the note on 1 Timothy 6. Here the striking point is that slaves are addressed directly as moral agents whose conduct can adorn the teaching about God, in a society that often regarded them as property.
cultural:
The key word of the chapter comes from the Greek family of sōphrōn, meaning sensible, self-controlled, sound-minded. It appears in some form in verses 2, 4, 5, 6, and 12, applied to every group. Self-control was one of the four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy, widely admired, and Paul's lists would have sounded respectable to Greek ears. But the reason he gives is not philosophical. It is the appearing of God's grace in Christ.

The instructions for older women (verses 3-5) give them a teaching role: they are to be “teachers of good” who train younger women. In a world where older women's influence operated mainly within households, this was a real ministry, and the warning against being slanderers and addicted to wine addresses common failings attributed to older women in ancient comic and moral literature. The expectations for younger women (love husbands and children, self-control, purity, managing the household, kindness, submission) matched the ideals of respectable Roman households. Titus himself, still relatively young, is to be an example in good works and sound speech.
literary: The chapter has two main parts and a closing command. Verses 1-10 give instructions to groups in the church, introduced by the charge to teach what accords with sound doctrine. Each group receives a short list of virtues, and three of the sections end with a purpose clause (“so that…”) explaining the effect on outsiders. Verses 11-14 then give the theological ground, beginning with “For”. This is one of the densest gospel summaries in Paul, framed by two appearings: grace has appeared (verse 11), and believers await the glorious appearance of Christ (verse 13). Between them lies the present age, in which grace instructs believers how to live. Verse 15 closes by repeating the charge to teach, encourage, and rebuke with authority. The chapter's structure itself makes the point: ethics rests on the gospel.

outline.t: Older men, older women, and younger women
Younger men and Titus as an example
The grace of God has appeared

doctrines.note: “The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone” (verse 11). Grace does not only forgive; it “instructs us to renounce ungodliness” (verse 12). Salvation includes being trained into a new way of life.

Most translations and interpreters read verse 13 as calling Jesus Christ “our great God and Savior”, one of the clearest statements of Christ's deity in the New Testament. A minority reading takes it as referring to God and to Christ separately, though the Greek grammar favors a single person.
Christ “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” (verse 14). Redemption means release by payment, and its purpose is a purified people, zealous for good deeds.
Believers live “in the present age” while awaiting “the blessed hope” of Christ's glorious appearing (verses 12-13). The future appearing gives shape and urgency to present conduct.

words.note: Paideuō, to train, instruct, or discipline, the word used for bringing up and educating a child. In verse 12 grace is the tutor. It is striking that the teacher of godly living is not law but grace, the undeserved favor of God that has appeared in Christ.

Epiphaneia, appearing or manifestation, from which comes the English word epiphany. Greek writers used it for a visible intervention by a god and for the ceremonial arrival of a ruler. In verse 13 it names Christ's return in glory, and the related verb in verse 11 describes the first appearing of grace in his coming.

Periousios, one's own special possession, found only here in the New Testament. It echoes the Greek Old Testament's description of Israel as God's treasured possession among the nations (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6). The church, made up of Jews and Gentiles, now shares that identity.

Sōphrōn, self-controlled or sensible, and its related forms run throughout the chapter (verses 2, 4, 5, 6, and 12). The word describes a sound, balanced mind that governs desires. It is the virtue asked of every group, old and young, men and women.

christ: Verses 11-14 set the whole Christian life between two appearings of Christ. His first coming was the appearing of God's grace, bringing salvation to everyone; his return will be the “glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (verse 13), a phrase most readers take as a direct confession of his deity. In between, he is at work shaping a people. He “gave Himself for us” (verse 14), echoing his own words about giving his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45), in order to redeem from lawlessness and to purify a people for his own possession, language God used of Israel at Sinai. The chapter shows who Christ is (God and Savior), what he has done (given himself to redeem), and what he is doing (making a people zealous for good).

hard.q: Does verse 5 require wives to submit to their husbands today, and how should the household instructions be applied?
hard.a:
Paul asks younger women to be “submissive to their own husbands” so that the word of God is not discredited (verse 5). Christians who share the same confession of faith read this in different ways, and it is a second-order question.

The complementarian reading holds that a wife's submission to her husband is a lasting pattern for Christian marriage, not only a concession to Roman custom. Its strongest arguments are that Paul elsewhere grounds the pattern in Christ's relationship to the church (Ephesians 5:22-33), that the husband's headship is defined by self-giving love rather than domination, and that the call is addressed to wives' own willing response, not to husbands as a right to enforce. The egalitarian reading holds that Paul applies the gospel within the household codes of his culture, and that the purpose clause shows his aim: to avoid discrediting the gospel among outsiders who expected such behavior. Its strongest arguments are that Ephesians 5:21 introduces the household instructions with mutual submission, that the same letter's instructions to slaves are no longer taken as endorsing slavery, and that where culture no longer reads mutual partnership as disgrace, the same missionary concern may point toward a partnership of equals.

Both readings agree that Paul's instructions aim at the gospel's reputation, that no instruction here licenses abuse or harshness, and that every believer, in every station, is called to self-control, kindness, and good works grounded in the grace of God.

questions: Paul says grace trains us to live. How is being trained by grace different from being pressured by rules?
Which of the instructions to your own age and stage of life do you find hardest, and why?
Paul wants believers' ordinary conduct to make the gospel attractive. What in your daily life might adorn the teaching about God, or discredit it?
